result.summary: A collection of short poems attributed to Homer: begging songs, prayers, curses on potters, a tomb inscription, and a riddle exchange with fishermen. They are occasional verses tied to towns of Asia Minor such as Cyme and Smyrna.

scenes.title: Pleas for hospitality at Cyme
scenes.summary: The poet asks the people of Cyme for a home and alms, then prays to reach a town of righteous men.
scenes.stakes: The wandering poet risks going without shelter and charity.

scenes.title: Bronze maiden on Midas's tomb
scenes.summary: A bronze statue speaks, declaring it will mark the tomb of Midas as long as nature endures.

scenes.title: Complaint against Smyrna and Cyme
scenes.summary: The poet laments the fate dealt him because Smyrna's people scorned the Muses' gift of song, and resolves to leave Cyme.
scenes.stakes: His disappointment and exile after being scorned.

scenes.title: Heart of man and sea prayer
scenes.summary: A saying about the human heart, then a prayer to Poseidon for safe voyage and revenge on a deceiver.
scenes.stakes: Danger at sea and the poet's wish for justice against a deceiver.

scenes.title: Short sayings and prayers
scenes.summary: Brief verses on Earth, sailors and strangers, pines of Ida, dogs, a prayer for an old lover, and what makes life good.

scenes.title: The Kiln, a curse on potters
scenes.summary: The poet offers to sing for potters, asks Athena's help, and threatens them with destructive spirits, Circe and Centaurs if they cheat him.
scenes.stakes: The potters' wares and the poet's payment.

scenes.title: Begging songs at the door
scenes.summary: Singers go house to house, blessing a wealthy home with the swallow song and asking for gifts.
scenes.stakes: Whether the household will give gifts.

scenes.title: Riddle with the fishermen
scenes.summary: Homer asks fishermen about their catch and they answer with a riddle about lice; he replies about their poverty.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable saying about the unfathomable human heart.
Famous epitaph promising Midas's tomb will endure as long as nature.
Opening of the swallow song, a famous begging song.

analysis.text: The poems center on hospitality, the wandering poet's dependence on strangers, and divine punishment of those who wrong guests.
These short pieces are later attributions, drawn from the ancient Life of Homer, and reflect itinerant singers' occasional verse in Ionian Greece.

legacy.text: The swallow song is a well-known example of Greek folk begging songs (the chelidonisma), still echoed in later spring customs.

fun_facts.text: Most of these epigrams are preserved in the pseudo-Herodotean Life of Homer, not in the epics.

language_notes.text: "Stranger's dole" means alms or charity given to a wanderer; the poet is asking the citizens for support.
Cyme is called a "maiden" because the city was said to be named for a female figure; Hermus is a river of Asia Minor.
"Riders on wanton horses" means spirited, unruly horses; the Phricon people are Aeolian Greek settlers in Asia Minor.
"Daughters of Zeus" are the Muses, goddesses of song and poetry.
"Contrived my fate" means the man's scornful words caused the poet's misfortune; the translator's note marks the referent as obscure.
"Sound" here means to measure the depth of, as with a sounding line; hence "unfathomable."
Helicon is a mountain in Boeotia, associated with Poseidon here as well as with the Muses.
Zeus is lord of guests (Zeus Xenios), protector of hospitality; cheating a guest offends him.
"Honey-hearted" is a compound epithet meaning sweet at its core; "intractable" means hard to work or cultivate.
The pine is addressed as if it were a person; the verse seems to refer to pine wood being cut for ships or weapons, with a better "fruit" being iron.
The Cebrenians were people of the Troad near Ida. The line prophesies iron mining once they hold the land.
"Dote on" means be foolishly fond of; "powers dulled" means the old men's bodily vigor has faded.
Shatter, Smash, Charr, Crash and Crudebake are translator's renderings of the demons' Greek names, each describing a way pots are ruined in firing.
The kiln is compared to a horse's jaw crunching, meaning it should crush the pots like teeth grinding food.
Heracles fought and killed many Centaurs in his labors; Chiron, the wise Centaur, was a notable exception to their wildness.
"Open of yourselves" means open by your own accord, as if the doors could respond to the singers' call.
Pottage is a thick porridge or stew; here it is made of barley and sesame, a festive dish the singers ask for.
The singers compare themselves to the swallow, whose yearly return heralds spring. This is why such begging songs were called swallow songs (chelidonisma).
The fishermen's riddle: the lice they picked from their clothes and killed were left behind, while those they could not catch they carried home.
Homer understands the riddle and replies that their fathers were poor, owning neither land nor flocks, hence their lice.

context_notes.text: Midas was a legendary king of Phrygia. This epigram is supposedly inscribed on his tomb, spoken by a bronze maiden statue.
Poseidon, god of the sea, was also called the earth-shaker, as he was thought to cause earthquakes.
Zeus was protector of strangers and guests (Zeus Xenios), so wronging a traveler or suppliant risked divine punishment.
Cronos was the father of Zeus; "Son of Cronos" is a standard title for Zeus as sender of weather.
Athena was patron goddess of crafts, including pottery, so she is the natural one to invoke.
Circe was a sorceress, daughter of the Sun, known for turning men into beasts with drugs and spells.
A lacuna is a gap in the surviving text, where lines have been lost.
Wishing good fortune on the son's bride is part of the blessing the singers offer in exchange for gifts.
The begging song promises blessings for a gift and, in the next line, a departure without one; refusal may bring a threat.

literary_notes.text: The bronze statue speaks in the first person, giving a voice to an inanimate object, as in many inscriptions.
The monument will last as long as rivers, sun and moon endure, using impossible-seeming permanence to stress eternity.
The poet predicts that the scornful man will one day regret his words, hinting at later vindication.
The poet addresses Thestorides directly, turning a general maxim into a personal accusation.
Calling the deceiver a wretch and invoking Zeus's protection of guests turns the prayer into a moral curse.
The speaker addresses Earth directly as a queen, honoring her and reflecting on her uneven treatment of people.
Sailors are likened to shy sea-fowl, stressing their restless, unsettled and vulnerable lives.
Children are called a man's crown and a city's towers, presenting them as honor and protection.
Pot-breaking forces become named demons summoned like warriors, with names that mimic their destructive work.
The curse claims a moral purpose, teaching honesty, while wishing painful disfigurement on the potters.
Wealth, Mirth and Peace are treated as guests who enter the house, and the doors are addressed as if they could obey.
The singers liken their yearly visit to the swallow's return, presenting themselves as welcome, harmless harbingers of good fortune.
The paradoxical answer hides a plain fact, making a joke of the fishermen's poverty and inviting Homer's wit.
